core: The Roman Republic, traditionally founded in 509 BCE after the overthrow of the monarchy, and its mixed constitution: the Senate, two annually elected consuls, popular assemblies, tribunes of the plebs with veto power, and a strictly time-limited emergency dictatorship

The Conflict of the Orders between patricians and plebeians and the reforms it produced: the Twelve Tables (c. 450 BCE), the tribunate, plebeian access to the consulship (after 367 BCE), and binding plebeian legislation (287 BCE)
Mediterranean expansion and the Punic Wars against Carthage (First 264-241 BCE, Second 218-201 BCE with Hannibal and the Battle of Zama 202 BCE, Third 149-146 BCE ending in Carthage's destruction)
The centrality of enslavement to Roman society and economy: conquest produced large numbers of enslaved captives who labored on estates, in mines, and in households with no legal freedom

The crisis of the Republic and transition to Empire: the Gracchi, Marius and Sulla, the First Triumvirate (60 BCE), Caesar crossing the Rubicon (49 BCE) and made dictator for life, his assassination (15 March 44 BCE), the Second Triumvirate, Actium (31 BCE), and Augustus as first emperor (27 BCE)
The Pax Romana (c. 27 BCE - 180 CE), Roman law (Twelve Tables through the later Code of Justinian), and Roman engineering (roads, gravity-fed aqueducts on arches, concrete)

The spread of Christianity in the empire: origins in the eastern provinces (1st century CE), persecution (Nero 64 CE; Diocletian 303-311), legalization under Constantine (Edict of Milan, 313 CE), and establishment as the official religion under Theodosius I (380 CE)

The division of the empire and the two 'falls': the permanent division after Theodosius I (395 CE), the traditional end of the Western Roman Empire (476 CE, Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus), and the survival of the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire until 1453 (Ottoman capture of Constantinople under Mehmed II)
supporting: The mixed constitution was later admired as a balance of monarchic (consuls), aristocratic (Senate), and democratic (assemblies) elements, though wealth and birth weighted participation and a narrow elite dominated
The Byzantine (eastern Roman) Empire preserved Roman law and Greek learning, reached a height under Justinian (r. 527-565 CE), and continued to identify as Roman
Historians emphasize there was no single, exact 'fall' of Rome; Roman authority faded gradually in the west and Roman culture persisted in successor kingdoms

claims.claim: By tradition, Romans overthrew their monarchy and established a republic in 509 BCE, governed by the Senate, two consuls elected each year, and popular assemblies, with a single dictator appointed only for strictly limited emergencies.

Roman society was divided into patricians (an aristocratic elite) and plebeians (common citizens); in the Conflict of the Orders the plebeians won the Twelve Tables (c. 450 BCE), tribunes who could veto actions harmful to plebeians, a requirement after 367 BCE that one consul be a plebeian, and, by 287 BCE, plebeian assembly laws binding on all citizens.

Rome fought three Punic Wars against Carthage: the First (264-241 BCE), after which Rome annexed Sicily; the Second (218-201 BCE), in which Hannibal invaded Italy but was defeated at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE; and the Third (149-146 BCE), in which Rome destroyed the city of Carthage.
Enslavement was central to Roman society: conquest produced large numbers of enslaved people who labored on agricultural estates, in mines, and in households and had no legal freedom.

The Republic collapsed amid civil war: the Gracchi were killed by senators; Marius and Sulla marched on Rome; the First Triumvirate formed in 60 BCE; Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, became dictator for life (dictator perpetuo) in 44 BCE, and was assassinated by senators on 15 March 44 BCE.

After Caesar's death, Octavian formed the Second Triumvirate (43 BCE) with Antony and Lepidus, defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the naval Battle of Actium in 31 BCE, and in 27 BCE took the honorific Augustus while holding supreme power, effectively becoming the first Roman emperor and ending the Republic.

The Pax Romana was a period of relative internal peace and stability across the empire, conventionally lasting from the reign of Augustus (from 27 BCE) to the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE, and was accompanied by extensive road-building (on the order of tens of thousands of miles).

Roman engineers built gravity-fed aqueducts that carried water into cities using the arch, and employed concrete and waterproof cement to master difficult terrain; the first aqueduct serving Rome, the Aqua Appia, dates to 312 BCE.

Christianity emerged in the empire in the first century CE and was periodically persecuted (under Nero in 64 CE and Diocletian in 303-311); the emperor Constantine's Edict of Milan in 313 CE made Christianity legal, and Roman law was later codified in the East as the Code of Justinian in the sixth century.

In 380 CE the emperor Theodosius I made Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire; Theodosius (r. 379-395 CE) was the last emperor to rule a united empire, and after his death in 395 CE the empire was divided permanently between his two sons.

The Western Roman Empire is traditionally dated to have ended in 476 CE, when the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, and made himself King of Italy; OpenStax stresses there was no exact single date of the empire's 'fall' and that the eastern half survived into the fifteenth century.

The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire, centered on Constantinople, continued to identify as Roman and reached a height under Justinian (r. 527-565 CE); it fell in 1453, when the Ottoman Turks under Mehmed II captured Constantinople, ending the Byzantine state.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The 'fall of Rome' has no single agreed date, and 476 CE is a convention rather than a precise event.
positions: The traditional endpoint of the Western Roman Empire is 476 CE, when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus.

OpenStax notes 'there was no exact date when the Roman Empire fell' and that even 476 'may be arbitrary,' because Roman authority faded gradually and Roman culture persisted in successor kingdoms; the eastern empire continued until 1453.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents 476 CE as the traditional/conventional end of the WESTERN empire, explicitly notes there was no single dramatic collapse, and contrasts it with the eastern (Byzantine) empire's survival until 1453 - so learners do not mistake 476 for the end of all Roman rule.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The dates of the Second Triumvirate and Caesar's dictatorship vary slightly by source in how they are framed.
positions: OpenStax dates the (formally recognized) Second Triumvirate to 43 BCE and the Battle of Philippi to 42 BCE.
World History Encyclopedia gives Caesar the title dictator perpetuo (dictator for life) in 44 BCE and his assassination on 15 March 44 BCE.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the secure, widely agreed anchor dates - First Triumvirate 60 BCE, Rubicon 49 BCE, Caesar's assassination 15 March 44 BCE, Actium 31 BCE, Augustus 27 BCE - and attributes them to the sources that state them.

sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 1: to 1500 - 6.4 The Roman Republic
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed open survey text. Supports: the Republic declared in 509 BCE after the overthrow of the Etruscan monarchy; government by Senate, two consuls, public assemblies, and tribunes with veto power; patricians vs plebeians; the Twelve Tables published c. 450 BCE; one consul required to be plebeian after 367 BCE; plebeian assembly laws binding on all citizens by 287 BCE; the Punic Wars - First (264-241 BCE, Sicily annexed), Second (218-201 BCE, Hannibal's invasion, Zama 202 BCE), Third (146 BCE, Carthage destroyed); enslavement in Roman society; the Gracchi killed by senators; Marius's army reforms; Sulla's march on Rome and dictatorship; the First Triumvirate (60 BCE). sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 1: to 1500 - 6.5 The Age of Augustus
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: the Second Triumvirate (43 BCE, formally recognized by the Senate) of Octavian, Antony, and Lepidus; the Battle of Philippi (42 BCE) against Caesar's assassins; the naval Battle of Actium (31 BCE) where Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra, who then died by suicide; Octavian in 27 BCE 'restoring' the Republic while in fact inaugurating the Empire as emperor; the Senate granting the title Augustus; the principate (from Princeps Senatus). sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 1: to 1500 - 7.4 Religion in the Roman Empire
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: Christianity emerging in the first century CE within Rome's diverse religious landscape; persecution under Nero (64 CE, blamed for the fire in Rome) and Diocletian (303-311, focused on destroying churches); Decius's universal-sacrifice edict (250 CE); Constantine attributing his 312 victory to the Christian God and issuing the Edict of Milan (313 CE) establishing toleration so Christianity was no longer illegal; and the government advocating monotheism from Constantine's time. Fetched via WebFetch (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-19. Reference only; facts synthesized, wording original.

sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 1: to 1500 - 10.2 The Byzantine Empire and Persia
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: the Byzantine (eastern Roman) Empire centered on Constantinople; the emperor Justinian (r. 527-565 CE), a devout Christian who commissioned the Hagia Sophia and the Code of Justinian (compiling and reconciling Roman law issued since the early second century, preserved in Latin); Belisarius's reconquests (Rome occupied 536). Establishes the survival of the Roman state in the East. Fetched via WebFetch (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-19. Reference only; facts synthesized, wording original.

sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 1: to 1500 - 13.1 The Post-Roman West in the Early Middle Ages
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: the traditional end of the Western Roman Empire fixed at 476, when the German general Odoacer deposed the emperor Romulus Augustulus and made himself King of Italy; the explicit caution that 'there was no exact date when the Roman Empire fell' and that 476 'may be arbitrary'; that Germanic peoples who settled in the former empire were not hostile to its culture, which lasted longer than Roman political authority; and that the eastern half did not collapse until the fifteenth century. sourceRecords.title: Pax Romana
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry. Supports that the Pax Romana was a period of relative peace and stability across the Roman Empire lasting over 200 years, beginning with the reign of Augustus (27 BCE - 14 CE) and effectively ending after the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE, accompanied by extensive infrastructure including over fifty thousand miles of roads and safer seas for trade. Fetched via WebFetch (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-19. Copyrighted reference work; facts used, wording original.

sourceRecords.title: Roman Aqueduct
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry. Supports that Roman aqueducts moved water by gravity along a regular gradient using the arch, employing new materials such as concrete and waterproof cement to overcome difficult terrain; and that the first aqueduct serving Rome was the Aqua Appia (312 BCE), with later examples such as the Aqua Marcia (144-140 BCE) and the Pont du Gard (c. 50 CE). Fetched via WebFetch (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-19. Copyrighted reference work; facts used, wording original.

sourceRecords.title: Julius Caesar
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry. Supports the First Triumvirate with Pompey and Crassus (60 BCE); Caesar crossing the Rubicon with his legions and marching on Rome (49 BCE), an act of war; his title Dictator Perpetuus (dictator for life) in 44 BCE; and his assassination on 15 March 44 BCE by senators including Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus, stabbed at the base of Pompey's statue. sourceRecords.title: 1453: The Fall of Constantinople
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia article. Supports that Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453 to Ottoman forces under Sultan Mehmed II, who used powerful cannons to breach the Theodosian Walls; that the Byzantine emperor Constantine XI died defending it; and that this ended the Byzantine Empire after more than 1,100 years as its capital. sourceRecords.title: Theodosius I
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry. Confirms Theodosius I reigned 379-395 CE and was the last emperor to rule a united Roman Empire, after whose death (395 CE) the empire was divided permanently. The article documents his establishment of Nicene Christianity as the official state religion (the Edict of Thessalonica, 380 CE); this 380 CE date was additionally corroborated via web search against multiple secondary references.
